Comparación de métodos de reducción de dimensión en modeolo FAVAR para el pronóstico de la inflación PCA vs. RPCA (y talvez UMAP).

Dylan Benavides

2025-09-09

# Función para pronosticar la variación interanual del IPC:
# Aquí yoy es: year-over-year

calc.yoy <- function(observed, forecasted) {
  # observed: inflaciones mensuales observadas (12 - n)
  # forecasted: inflaciones mensuales pronosticadas (n)
  
  months <- c(observed, forecasted)
  
  yoy <- prod(1 + months) - 1
  return(yoy)
}

# Función para revisar si las series de un dataset son estacionarias con 90% de confianza o no:

is.stationary <- function(x) {
  x <- na.omit(x)
  test <- ur.df(x, type = "drift", selectlags = "AIC")
  tau2 <- test@teststat[1]         
  crit10 <- test@cval[1, "5pct"]  
  return(tau2 < crit10)
}

FAVAR con RPCA

La reducción de dimensión se hizo en Python con Riemannian Stats (solo está en python).

data <- read_csv("ffactors_ipc.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) #tabla generada en Python

# Aquí se guardan los factores extraídos de RPCA (esta parte del código fue ejecutada en python con el paquete Riemannian Stats).

colnames(data) <- c(paste0("F", 1:10),"inflation")

months <- c("Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun")
train.ends <-  171:176
true.values <- c(1.15, 1.25, 1.21, 0.37, -0.12, -0.22)

max.factors <- 8 #HIPERPARÁMETRO NO ASOCIADO AL VAR, SOLO ES LA CANTIDAD DE VARIABLES QUE SE INTRODUCEN AL VAR, EL % DE VARIANZA EXPLICADA POR LOS FACTORES VA AUMENTANDO CONFORME AUMENTA EL # DE VARIABLES, SIN EMBARGO, TAMPOCO ES ÚTIL UN MODELO VAR CON MUCHAS VARIABLES.

max.lags <- 4 #CANTIDAD DE REZAGOS, HAY CRITERIOS COMO AIC, BIC PAR VER EL ÓPTIMO (EL QUE MINIMICE EL AIC CREO)

# SE PUEDEN COMBINAR EN UNA BÚSQUEDA POR GRILLA

results.rmse <- data.frame()
results.forecasts <- data.frame()

for (r in 1:max.factors) {

  factors.r <- data[, paste0("F", 1:r)]
  VAR.data <- cbind(inflation = data$inflation, factors.r)
  final.ts <- ts(VAR.data, start = c(2010, 10), frequency = 12)

  for (p in 1:max.lags) {

    errors <- c()

    for (i in seq_along(train.ends)) {

      T.end <- train.ends[i]
      train <- as.data.frame(final.ts[1:T.end, ])
      var.model <- vars::VAR(train, p = p, type = "const")
      pred <- predict(var.model, n.ahead = 1)

      observed <- train$inflation[(T.end - 10):T.end]
      forecast.ipc <- pred$fcst$inflation[1, 1]
      forecast.yoy <- calc.yoy(observed, forecast.ipc)
      error <- forecast.yoy - true.values[i]
      errors <- c(errors, error)
      results.forecasts <- rbind(results.forecasts, 
                                 data.frame(
                                   factors = r,
                                   lag = p,
                                   month = months[i],
                                   forecast = forecast.yoy,
                                   actual = true.values[i],
                                   error = error))
      }

    rmse <- sqrt(mean(errors^2))
    results.rmse <- rbind(results.rmse,
                          data.frame(
                            factors = r,
                            lag = p,
                            rmse = rmse))
  }
}

# Pronósticos del mejor modelo

best.model <- results.rmse[which.min(results.rmse$rmse), ]
best.r <- best.model$factors
best.p <- best.model$lag
best.forecasts <- subset(results.forecasts, factors == best.r & lag == best.p)
best.forecasts
##     factors lag month   forecast actual       error
## 139       6   4   Jan  0.9517635   1.15 -0.19823646
## 140       6   4   Feb  0.8731684   1.25 -0.37683161
## 141       6   4   Mar  1.7175723   1.21  0.50757228
## 142       6   4   Apr  0.3173706   0.37 -0.05262939
## 143       6   4   May -0.0877728  -0.12  0.03222720
## 144       6   4   Jun -0.3448701  -0.22 -0.12487011
# Métricas

errors.best <- best.forecasts$error
rmse <- sqrt(mean(errors.best^2))
mae <- mean(abs(errors.best))
bias <- mean(errors.best)

performance.summary <- data.frame(
  model = "RPCA-FAVAR",
  factors = best.r,
  lag = best.p,
  RMSE = rmse,
  MAE = mae,
  Bias = bias)

performance.summary
##        model factors lag      RMSE       MAE        Bias
## 1 RPCA-FAVAR       6   4 0.2763845 0.2153945 -0.03546135

Modelo final RPCA (6 factores y 4 rezagos)

#MODELO CALIBRADO ENTRE COMILLAS
data <- read_csv("ffactors_ipc.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
colnames(data) <- c(paste0("F", 1:10), "inflation")
factors <- data[, paste0("F", 1:6)] # 6 factores
final.ts <- cbind(inflation = data$inflation,factors)
train <- as.data.frame(final.ts[1:171, ])
VAR.ts <- ts(train, start = c(2010, 10), frequency = 12)
var.model <- vars::VAR(VAR.ts, p = 4, type = "const") # 4 rezagos

prediction.var <- predict(var.model, n.ahead = 6, ci = 0.95)
prediction.var$fcst$inflation

# Raíces del polinomio característico:
roots(var.model)
##  [1] 0.9045156 0.9045156 0.7719631 0.7719631 0.7660677 0.7534106 0.7534106
##  [8] 0.7532242 0.7447616 0.7447616 0.6991242 0.6991242 0.6872490 0.6872490
## [15] 0.6773361 0.6773361 0.6722146 0.6722146 0.6379321 0.6379321 0.6175700
## [22] 0.6170543 0.6170543 0.4585297 0.3050386 0.3050386 0.2504558 0.2504558
# ¿Autocorrelación residual?
serial.test(var.model, lags.pt = 12, type = "PT.asymptotic")
## 
##  Portmanteau Test (asymptotic)
## 
## data:  Residuals of VAR object var.model
## Chi-squared = 535.15, df = 392, p-value = 1.922e-06
# ¿Heteroscedasticidad?
arch.test(var.model, lags.multi = 5, multivariate.only = TRUE)
## 
##  ARCH (multivariate)
## 
## data:  Residuals of VAR object var.model
## Chi-squared = 4171.3, df = 3920, p-value = 0.002661
# ¿Normalidad de los residuos?
normality.test(var.model, multivariate.only = TRUE)
## $JB
## 
##  JB-Test (multivariate)
## 
## data:  Residuals of VAR object var.model
## Chi-squared = 5517, df = 14, p-value < 2.2e-16
## 
## 
## $Skewness
## 
##  Skewness only (multivariate)
## 
## data:  Residuals of VAR object var.model
## Chi-squared = 330.41, df = 7, p-value < 2.2e-16
## 
## 
## $Kurtosis
## 
##  Kurtosis only (multivariate)
## 
## data:  Residuals of VAR object var.model
## Chi-squared = 5186.6, df = 7, p-value < 2.2e-16
# Pronóstico I Semestre 2025
prediction.var <- predict(var.model, n.ahead = 6, ci = 0.95)
plot(prediction.var, names = "inflation")

# Resultados:

# 1. Raíces del polinomio característico dentro del círculo unitario. VAR estable.
# 3. Hay autocorrelación residual
# 4. Hay heteroscedasticidad condicional
# 5. No hay normalidad

# Pronóstico de un mes para ver si coincide con el modelo calibrado:

pred <- predict(var.model, n.ahead = 1)
forecast.ipc <- pred$fcst$inflation[1, 1]
observed <- train$inflation[(171 - 10):171]
forecast.yoy <- calc.yoy(observed, forecast.ipc)
forecast.yoy
## [1] 0.9517635

Grafiquillo 2

Aquí se grafica el primer factor RPCA vs. todas las series del dataset inicial.

data0 <- read_xlsx("datos.xlsx", sheet = "datos")
dates <- data0$date
inflation <- data0$ipc_d11
data1 <- data0 %>% dplyr::select(-date, -ipc_d11)

data <- read_csv("ffactors_ipc.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

series.mat <- as.matrix(data1)
series.scaled <- scale(series.mat)   # media 0, sd 1
pc1 <- data[, 1]
pc1.scaled <- scale(pc1)

time.index <- dates
df.series <- data.frame(
  date   = rep(time.index, ncol(series.scaled)),
  value  = as.vector(series.scaled),
  series = rep(colnames(series.scaled), each = nrow(series.scaled))
)

df.pc1 <- data.frame(
  date   = time.index,
  value  = as.numeric(pc1.scaled),
  series = "PC1"
)

a2 <- ggplot() +

  geom_line(
    data = df.series,
    aes(x = date, y = value, group = series),
    color = "grey70",
    linewidth = 0.3,
    alpha = 0.6
  ) +

  geom_line(
    data = df.pc1,
    aes(x = date, y = value),
    color = "blue",
    linewidth = 1.5
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Standardized Series and First RPCA Factor",
    x = "Time",
    y = "Standardized values"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

a2
